html_body:
Pabrai Has Beaten The S&P Since 1999 — This Isn't About Stocks

The value legend's annual Berkshire-weekend interview skips the ticker talk and asks a harder question: are you living a life that's actually yours?

Episode: The Inner Scorecard w/ Mohnish Pabrai — 04 May 2024

Every year on Berkshire weekend, Stig Brodersen sits down with Mohnish Pabrai. This time he decided to be the person at the concert who shouts for a deep cut instead of the greatest hits. Borrowing a premise from a listener who once ended up next to Pabrai on a train by pure chance, Stig asked the kind of selfish, personal questions you'd put to a stranger you'll never see again — not what Pabrai is buying, but how he lives. The result is the rare value-investor interview with almost no tickers in it, and possibly the most useful one.

TL;DR

Pabrai's flagship fund has compounded at 11.7% a year since its 1999 inception — roughly four points ahead of the S&P 500, turning a single dollar into $12.51 against the index's $4.72. (Stig discloses he is himself an investor in the fund.) But the numbers are the setup, not the story. The real subject is the “inner scorecard”: Warren Buffett's idea that a life worth living is one you grade by your own standards, not the world's applause. Over the hour Pabrai gets into the decisions that made him happier, how he grades the people around him, why he prefers bridge to poker, and why he and Buffett both refuse to take notes.

What The Inner Scorecard Actually Means

Buffett's test goes like this: would you rather be the world's best investor and have everyone think you're the worst, or the world's worst and have everyone think you're the best? Your answer tells you which scorecard you're keeping. The inner one measures you against your own values; the outer one measures you against other people's opinions.

Pabrai builds the whole conversation around living a “congruent” life — one where what you claim to value and how you actually spend your days line up. That can sound like a self-help detour until you remember what value investing demands. A concentrated investor who buys what's cheap and unloved will, by definition, look wrong for long stretches. If you're keeping an outer scorecard, you can't survive that; the crowd's disapproval will shake you out at the worst possible moment. The inner scorecard is the psychological machinery that lets you hold a position while everyone around you is laughing at it.

Grade The Person, Skip The Notes

Two of the episode's threads are deceptively practical. The first is Buffett's exercise for grading people: pick the person you'd most want to be, write down the specific qualities that make you admire them, and then — the hard part — go install those qualities in yourself. It reframes character as something you assemble on purpose rather than something you're simply born with.

The second is stranger: neither Buffett nor Pabrai takes notes. In a culture that fetishizes second brains and note-taking systems, that's close to heresy. The implied logic is that the ideas worth acting on are the ones you can't forget — if you needed to write it down to remember it, it probably wasn't a strong enough signal to bet real money on. It's a filter disguised as a bad habit.

Why He'd Rather Play Bridge Than Poker

The bridge-over-poker preference is the episode's most quietly revealing detail. Poker is a game of exploiting other people's mistakes under financial pressure, frequently by bluffing. Bridge is a partnership game of probability and communication, where you win by playing your cards well rather than by breaking the person across the table. That Pabrai gravitates to the second says something about temperament: he'd rather be measured against the odds than against an opponent. It's the inner scorecard showing up at the card table.

What A Retail Investor Should Steal From This

Here's the uncomfortable takeaway. The 11.7% didn't come from a formula you can copy — it came from a strategy Pabrai could actually stick to because it fit who he is. Most investors lose not because their ideas are bad but because they can't hold them; they abandon a thesis the moment the market disagrees, because their scorecard lives outside themselves.

So before you copy anyone's portfolio, copy the prior step: define your own scorecard. Decide what you're optimizing for, what you're willing to look wrong about, and for how long. Pabrai's clearest evidence that he's living his own answer isn't in the fund at all — it's the Dakshana Foundation, which he funds to coach gifted, low-income students in India into the country's top universities. That is what a congruent life looks like once the compounding is done: the scorecard that counts is the one nobody else is keeping.

  • Mohnish Pabrai's Dakshana Foundation
